# 2015B Question 15 {.unnumbered}

::: {.exam-question}
## Question {.question-label}

[**Discuss**]{.task-verb} the prevention of electrical shock in the operating theatre.
:::

:::: {#answer-structure}

## Suggested Structure

[**Discuss**]{.task-verb} prevention through the conditions required for current to pass through a person. Explain electrical supply and equipment protections with their rationale and limitations, distinguishing macroshock from microshock.

::: {.structure-headings}
### Shock Circuit and Danger Thresholds

### Residual Current Devices

### Isolated Supply and Line Isolation Monitoring

### Equipotential Earthing

### Equipment Classes and Protected Areas
:::

::::

## Examiner Comments

::: {.examiner-comments}
**23%** of candidates achieved a pass in this question

Several candidates failed badly. Most candidates attempted to open with a definition of macroshock and microshock, frequently quoting the typical currents required to induce ventricular fibrillation. A discussion of operating room electrical supply design features, followed by electrical device design features was expected. The rationale behind these designs and their limitations was also expected.

Most candidates had only a superficial understanding of electrical shock prevention. Several candidates could (correctly) list some safety features, but contributed little more. A discussion of diathermy and burns related phenomena was not required. Only a handful of candidates knew that diathermy produced an alternating current at a frequency several orders of magnitude greater than that of mains supply, or why the frequency of the current was important.
:::
